title: Baseline and Bonuses for the I Do and We Do phases of a lesson
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton sets out an order of priority for developing the modelling phase of maths lessons, drawing on watching over a hundred lessons a month. For each of the I Do and We Do he distinguishes a Baseline, the minimum to see benefit, from Bonuses to add later. The I Do baseline is a clear, concise, teacher-led live explanation after prerequisites are assessed, with bonuses of checks for listening, Silent Teacher and Turn and Talk rehearsal. The We Do baseline is a mini-whiteboard check, with bonuses of Step-by-Step, the Tick Trick and Variations. He advises nailing the baselines first, which he estimates gets about 70 percent of the way, before adding the bonuses.
points: Barton separates Baselines from Bonuses so departments can sequence which modelling techniques to adopt first.
A teacher-led, rehearsed, live-modelled explanation is preferred over co-constructed questioning or clicking through animated slides.
Mini-whiteboards give data from every student, which circulation, cold call and hands-up cannot.
Step-by-Step, the Tick Trick and Variation questions deepen the We Do by showing the structure of working and the critical features that change.
Adopt the baselines first, since they are worth about 70 percent of the benefit.
quotes: I advise assessing prerequisite knowledge before an I Do. This is important because it means we do not have to do so during the I Do. Instead, we can focus on giving a clear explanation that builds upon what we have established students already know.

Live modelling allows the teacher to control the pace and students’ attention better and helps reduce the disconnect between what the teacher is doing on the board and what students will be asked to do shortly themselves.
Dropping in some checks for listening into our I Do gives us data on whether students are listening, helps sustain their attention, and provides a confidence boost to students who most need it.

A Turn and Talk rehearsal after the I Do can be a great way to bridge the gap. Give students, say, 10 seconds each to talk through the steps of the worked example with their partner, and then swap roles.
We have just introduced a new idea and need data immediately on whether students are on the path to understanding. Circulation takes too long, Cold Call and hands-up give us just one data point.

Step-by-Step gives us the best chance of seeing our students’ work, allows us to diagnose exactly where in the process students are struggling, and gives all students several opportunities to feel successful instead of just one if they do the question from start to finish.
This forces students to focus on the structure and working out instead of the final answer, helping to build solid foundations for setting their work out going forward.
